details:
**Nora slams the door**
Henrik Ibsen's 1879 play ends with Nora Helmer leaving her husband Torvald and their children, and the final stage direction is the sound of the front door slamming shut. This "door slam heard round the world" made the play a landmark of early feminism, and it is the most common giveaway.

**Krogstad's blackmail**
Nils Krogstad, a lawyer and clerk at the bank Torvald has just begun managing, is about to be fired. Years earlier he lent Nora money, so he blackmails her, threatening to expose her secret unless she makes sure he keeps his job. Dr. Rank calls him "morally diseased," and he finally reveals everything in a letter he drops into Torvald's locked letterbox.

**The forged signature and the trip to Italy**
Years before the play, Torvald fell seriously ill from overwork (just after the birth of their son Ivar), and doctors said he needed a year in Italy to recover. Nora secretly borrowed the money from Krogstad by forging her dying father's signature on the bond as guarantor. She has been paying it back in secret, partly by working as a copyist, and she lied to her friend that the money came from her father.

**Dr. Rank**
A family friend who is dying of inherited syphilis, euphemistically called "tuberculosis of the spine" and blamed on his father's sins. He confesses his love for Nora, which upsets her, and announces his coming death by leaving visiting cards marked with black crosses in the Helmers' letterbox.

**The tarantella**
Nora rehearses the wild Italian tarantella for a fancy-dress ball at the Stenborgs' apartment upstairs, wearing a Neapolitan costume. She dances it violently ("I must, I must") and insists Torvald coach her, so that he will not open the letterbox containing Krogstad's letter. Afterward she reckons she has "thirty-one hours to live."

**"Little squirrel" and "little skylark"**
Torvald's condescending pet names for Nora, along with "songbird" and "Miss Sweet Tooth." He also scolds her as a "spendthrift" for spending too much on Christmas presents, showing how he treats her like a child or a pet.

**The macaroons**
Torvald has forbidden Nora to eat sweets, but she secretly eats macaroons and lies to his face when he asks whether she has had any. This small deception in the opening scene foreshadows her larger secrets.

**Kristine Linde**
Nora's childhood friend, a childless widow who arrives in town looking for work after years of caring for her sick mother and younger brothers. Nora confides the loan to her. Mrs. Linde gets a job at the bank, and as Krogstad's former love she agrees to marry him; she convinces him to stop the blackmail but still lets the truth come out so the Helmers can face it.

**"The most wonderful thing" (the miracle)**
Nora hopes that "something glorious," a miracle, will happen: that Torvald will take the blame for her forgery himself. When he instead turns on her and only forgives her once he is safe, she says she no longer believes in wonderful things. The play's last line is Torvald's hopeful question, "The most wonderful thing of all—?", just before the door slams.

**Nora's "settling of accounts"**
In the final scene Nora sits Torvald down and points out that in eight years of marriage they have never had a serious conversation. She says she has lived by "performing tricks" for him and for her father, who treated her as a doll, that their home has been a playroom in which she was his "doll-wife," and that she must leave to become a free human being and educate herself.

**Christmas Eve setting**
The play opens on Christmas Eve as a porter delivers a Christmas tree, which Nora tells the maid Helene to hide from the children until it is decorated. Torvald recalls how the previous Christmas Nora spent three weeks shut away making decorations for the tree. The children's old nurse Anne-Marie also appears.

**Torvald Helmer**
Nora's husband, a newly promoted bank manager who cares most about respectability. He claims that "nearly all young criminals have had lying mothers," which haunts Nora. When Krogstad returns the bond, Torvald burns the papers and declares himself "saved," revealing his selfishness.

**The alternate German ending**
The German actress Hedwig Niemann-Raabe refused to play a mother who abandons her children, so Ibsen reluctantly wrote an alternate ending in which Torvald leads Nora to the children's bedroom and she collapses instead of leaving. Ibsen called this version a "barbaric outrage."

**Sequels and adaptations**
Lucas Hnath's A Doll's House, Part 2 (2017) has Nora return fifteen years later and meet the nurse Anne Marie. Elfriede Jelinek's What Happened after Nora Left Her Husband; or, Pillars of Society has Nora become a factory worker, and Eleanor Marx and Israel Zangwill wrote the parody A Doll's House Repaired. A 2023 minimalist Broadway production starred Jessica Chastain sitting in a chair on a revolving stage.

**Lu Xun's speech and Claire Bloom's memoir**
In a 1923 speech, "What Happens After Nora Leaves Home?", the Chinese writer Lu Xun argued that without economic independence Nora would either fall into degradation or return home, and compared her situation to China's. The actress Claire Bloom titled her memoir about her marriage to Philip Roth Leaving a Doll's House.
